title: Blessing your children
hook: hands on heads each Friday night
tomorrow: the Torah says when to teach your kids. hint: not at a desk.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hard case: Maimonides and the Raavad, both keeping the parent in view. Honor with boundaries. Today, the gentlest thing hands do in a Jewish home.
screen: `HONOR WITH BOUNDARIES.` → `THE GENTLEST THING HANDS DO.`

segments.voice: A hand on top of the head is how people check for a fever, how a coach says good game, how a grandparent says hello without words. On Friday night, before the meal, some Jewish parents rest their hands on their children's heads and say a few lines from the Torah. Whose words are they, and why those?
screen: `A HAND ON THE HEAD.` → `FRIDAY NIGHT, BEFORE THE MEAL.` → `WHOSE WORDS?`

segments.voice: For sons, the words come from Genesis. Old Jacob, his eyes dim, is blessing his grandsons, Joseph's two boys, and he says Israel will bless its children with their names: "God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh." For daughters, a custom names the four mothers: may God make you like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah. Then some families add the blessing the priests gave in the Temple, from the book of Numbers: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee; The LORD make His face to shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee; The LORD lift up His countenance upon thee, and give thee peace." Why Ephraim and Manasseh, and not Abraham or Moses? One reading: they're brothers in Genesis who don't fight, and they grew up far from home, in Egypt, and stayed who they were. Now notice the senses in it. The weight of a hand. A parent's voice close enough to hear the breath. Some parents add a few quiet words of their own. And nothing has to be earned first: the hands come on a bad week too. Something to tell a friend: the blessing for sons is named for two grandsons, blessed by their grandfather.
screen: `SONS: LIKE EPHRAIM AND MANASSEH.` · `DAUGHTERS: LIKE THE FOUR MOTHERS.` · `THE PRIESTS' BLESSING, FROM NUMBERS.` · `NOTHING TO EARN FIRST.` · then, large: `HANDS ON HEADS.`

segments.voice: Rest one hand lightly on the top of your own head, or on the head of a child you love if one is beside you. Feel its weight, warm and still. Bring one child in your life to mind by name. If you pray, you can say the priests' words from Numbers for them; if not, simply hold them in mind under that hand.
screen: `A HAND, RESTING LIGHTLY.` · `ONE CHILD, BY NAME.` · `HOLD THEM THERE.`

segments.voice: Blessing your children: hands on heads on Friday night, with the Torah's words. Ephraim and Manasseh for sons, the four mothers for daughters.
Keep this one close: hands on heads, on a good week and a hard one. Five days into home and family.

chat.meaning: The words come from Genesis, where a grandfather blesses his grandsons. The custom sets no age for it.

Ephraim.meaning: Joseph's younger son, blessed by Jacob

Manasseh.meaning: Joseph's older son, blessed by Jacob

Rebekah.meaning: Isaac's wife, one of the four mothers

Leah.meaning: Jacob's wife, one of the four mothers
